Planned_Implementation:
PRESCRIBED FIRE PLAN
I. INTRODUCTION
Paul Makela of the Snake River Resource Area has requested our help in burning
through prescription approximately 50 acres of Juniper Seedlings on the East Jim
Sage Chaining Area. The objective of the burn is to remove the new encroaching
juniper and brush piles from the chaining. The site will be burned through It
has been determined that this would be the preferred method of maintaining the
chaining.
II. BURN AREA DESCRIPTION
LEGAL DESCRIPTION: COUNTY:
T. 15 S. R. 26 E. Section 08 Acres 50 Cassia
ELEVATION: ASPECT:
6500 Ft. East
ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION NUMBER:
East Jim Sage Chaining Maintenance EA # ID-020-94-017
TOPOGRAPHY:
mostly flat, rolling terrain 5 -15% slope
FUEL TYPEIDESCRIPTION:
chaining brush piles and juniper seedlings
III. OBJECTIVES
Removal of brush piles as a result of chaining and slow encroachment of new,
young juniper seedlings through burning.
IV. BURN PRESCRIPTION
                                                  ACCEPTABLE          PRESCRIPTION              RANGE
                                                        (low)                         (high)                         (desired)
Temperature                                35                               55                                    40
Relative Humidity                      40                               80                                    50
1 Hour Fuel Moisture                na                               na                                   na
Wind Speed                                  none
Wind Direction                            na                               na                                   na
V. FIRE BEHAVIOR
The fire should burn intensely consuming all dry and cured fuels at the site. The
brushpiles and dormant seedlings will be ignited with drip torches to promote a hot
fire of short duration to consume the fuel as soon as possible an lessen the impact on
other perennial vegetation in the chaining.
SMOKE MANAGEMENT
DISTANCE AND DIRECTION FROM SMOKE SENSITIVE AREAS:
The Craters of the Moon National Monument which is the closest Class I
Airshed lies approximately 66 miles North of the burn site. Interstate 84 is
approximately 22 miles North of the proposed site.
NECESSARY TRANSPORT WIND DIRECTION:
Any wind direction should be sufficient to transport the smoke away from the Class I
Airshed and not risk impacting traffic on Interstate 84; however, the amount of smoke
generated from the burn site should be very minimal and of short duration. It is
anticipated that this proposal would only have a limited, short duration impact.
VISIBILITY HAZARDS (roads, airports, etc. ):
Interstate 84
RESIDUAL SMOKE PROBLEMS: There are no anticipated problems.
SPECIAL CONSTRAINTS/CONSIDERATIONS: Interstate 84
VII. IGNITION SCHEDULING
SEASON: spring Date: 3/1 - 4/30 Time: 1200 - 1600
IGNITION METHOD: Drip Torches.
TYPE OF FIRE: individual
LENGTH OF IGNITION PHASE: 2 hours
VIII. PUBLIC INFORMATION
DAY OF BURN CONTACTS:
1. City of Malta 3. Power County
2. City of Rockland 4. Cassia County
IX. FIRING & HOLDING
FIRING PLAN: The crew will burn-out each existing pile and seedling.
The primary ignition should create an aggressive, hot fire of short
duration which will consume the majority of the fuel in within one hour.
POTENTIAL HOLDING PROBLEMS: There are no holding problems
anticipated because the project area has 8 - 12 inches of snow.
ESCAPE CONTINGENCY PLAN: In the event the fire should
escape all ignition will cease immediately. Personnel on the scene will
respond to the escaped fire and begin a coordinated direct suppression
effort. The Shoshone Dispatch will be immediately notified. The Burn
Boss will coordinate with Dispatch for additional crew needs.
Additional forces will be on stand-by in Burley in case of a escaped
fire. If the status of the stand-by help changes then Shoshone Dispatch
will immediately notify the Burn Boss.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS/HAZARDS: Crews will wear all their
Personal Protective Equipment including fire shelters, nomex shirt, gloves,
goggles, and helmets. The Burn Boss and crew members will maintain
visual and voice contact with each other.
In the event of an accident the Burn Boss will be notified. If the accident
is life threatening the Burn Boss will activate the Emergency Evacuation
Plan via the Shoshone BLM Dispatch.
An on-site briefing will take place the day of any activity. The Burn Boss
will conduct a critique when the project is completed.
X. PERSONNEL & EQUIPMENT
PRESCRIBED FIRE MANAGER: R. Mitchell
BURN BOSS: Mark Wiseman/ Dave Smith
PERSONNEL: 04
ENGINES: 0
XI. ESTIMATED COST
IGNITION HOLDING COSTS
Drip Torches, Fuel    $150.00
Support Vehicles      $120.00
TOTAL COSTS:             $270.00
All fire personnel costs will be paid from 2810 funds. Any equipment costs and
overtime will be paid from the benefitting activity.
Actual_Implementation:
On Thursday 2/19/98, Jim Tharp, Ecologist, and Kurt Pavlat,
Rangeland Mgmt. Spec. and I worked from approximately 10am to 4pm
burning young junipers that had survived the chaining or had
germinated since 1991. Where sufficient grasses, such as
bluebunch wheatgrass , western wheatgrass etc. or shrubs had
accumulated near the base of the seedlings/saplings, we probably
had fairly good success in charring cambium. We worked 2 areas. 
The northernmost zone, harbored less snow due
to its generally southeast exposure. It was also receiving fairly
heavy deer use on grass greenup and on some shrubs. The southern
unit contained more snow though we did have some success, again
where there were accumulated fine fuels. This area had been
worked in prior years.
We need to continue with several visits per year, working
designated patches systematically. It would be helpful to have
8-10 or more people with torches. We also discussed the
possibility of some limited prescribed burning (fall?), maybe 5-
10 acres a year. This would be much less labor intensive than
burning individual trees in winter, though would result in
mortality of some bitterbrush, sagebrush and fourwing.
On Thursday March 5, 1998 we resumed with burning junipers and
brush piles within the Jim Sage Chaining, using drip torches.
With six people, we were able to cover approximately 25-30 acres
along the northern portion, east of the leave area "peninsula&&.
We had best success with drip torches; Dave
Smith (burn boss) attempted using a propane burner, but this
proved too time-consuming, as it took too long to ignite the
fuels. In general, we felt we made substantial progress today,
again owing to the grass accumulated around the trees, and
generally clear skies , although clouds moved in later on.
If we could continue at this rate, using several personnel, we
could conceivably cover all or most of the chaining in a few more
trips.

The purpose of the proposed action is to reinstate fire as an ecological process within the sagebrush mosaic/juniper woodland
vegetation in Fisher Canyon. A fire plan has been developed to address this need. This EA analyzes the impacts of implementing
this plan. Decades of fire suppression, coupled with historic overgrazing (1870-1934) have significantly altered the presettlement
fire regimes of most High Desert plant communities over the past 100 years (Kauffman and Sapsis 1989). The current
abundance of shrubs and western juniper (Juniperus occidentalis) saplings and juveniles within Fisher Canyon represent a local
expression of this general trend.

Oregon Agricultural Research Center (EOARC).

Within this 16,000 acres (approximate) located on the South Steens Allotment fire has been
removed as a natural ecosystem function. Due to the mature and decadent vegetative stands
in this area, vegetative regeneration is necessary with stimulation occurring through fire.
Areas dominated by juniper on deep soil sites have priority for treatment by fire. The
second priority would be big sagebrush areas containing 5 percent or more canopy cover of
young juniper trees (determined by height and age class). In both of these communities plant
species diversity is being lost. The juniper dominated sites have only a limited number of
years when fire would be effective in reestablishing species and structural diversity without
long recovery periods. Prescribed fire will be restricted from mature juniper stands due to
the lack of fine fuels, severity of burn required to carry through crowns, and long recovery
time following a burn.
Resource Objectives and Desired Effects:
1. Maintain watershed integrity to enhance hydrologic function.
2. Achieve a mosaic of forage production and cover needs for wildlife and livestock.
3. Document the effects of fall burning on native vegetation.
4. Enhance the richness of plant and animal species.
5. Manage for natural succession by using fire in a role that it plays in the natural
ecological process on the Steens Mountain. Treatment will result in a desired mosaic
effect.
6. Fire Hazard reduction.

Objectives: The Proposed Action is to burn approximately 35 percent (3600 acres) of the Stonehouse Allotment.  The burns would be in mountain sagebrush-bunchgrass communities, aspen, remnant aspen, and wet meadow plant communities.  These burns would create a landscape mosaic within the treatment area of 40-55 percent of the mountain sagebrush-bunchgrass plant communities actually being burned and 45-60 percent of the mountain sagebrush-bunchgrass plant communities actually being burned and 45-60 percent unburned.  Forty percent or less of the wet meadow plant communities will actually be burned.  The aspen and remnant aspen plant communities identified for the fire reintroduction (130 acres) would require juniper cutting to allow these communities to burn.  These stands would be expected to have 90 to 100 percent burn and would require temporary net protective fences (8 feet in height) around them.
Planned_Implementation: The proposed action is the reintroduction of fire through prescribed burning on approximately 35 percent of the allotment 36000 acres, of which 500 acres is within the Wilderness Study Areas.  Most of the area proposed for reintroduction of fire is mountain big sagebrush-bunchgrass communities in an early transition state to juniper woodlands.

Objectives:
Control seral juniper on 60% of the area within the burn perimeter as measured by the percentage of canopy burned in pre and post fire plots.

--Maintain watershed function, stability, and reduce accelerated erosion by maintaining and increasing shrub and diverse herbaceous plant communities

--Restore suitability of mountain big sagebrush/bitterbrush-bunchgrass communities as sage grouse nesting habitat. 

--Improve wildlife habitat for sage grouse, elk, deer, antelope, migratory birds, small mammals, amphibians, reptiles by creating and maintaining vegetative mosaics.
Planned_Implementation: --Ignition is planned for late summer through fall, with a potential window occurring from August through October. The blackline ignition may occur as a separate operation, with a minimum of resources, if a window occurs in late fall or early spring. Ignition of the main unit would follow when the typical fall window is available.\r\n\r\n--Blackline divided into four sections, each expected to require 1 day to complete for a total of 4 days. Aerial ignition of interior is expected to require 2 days with a Heli torch. Use of a PSD device in marginal conditions would likely take longer.
Actual_Implementation: Prescribed burn began September 6, was completed on September 9 2008.\r\n\r\nTotal acreage burned was 3943 acres. As described, fire activity was most consistent in the shrub fuel model, where large pockets of Sage/Ceanothus were consumed. Over the remaining portions of the unit there were minimal surface fuels under juniper stands. In these areas fire consumption was low.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Observations indicate that all of the objectives either have been met or are trending upwards towards being met. Fire has been reintroduced, resulting in the opening of the juniper canopy allowing for a more diverse ecosystem. Within the monitoring plots, trees per acre have been reduced from 244 to 43 per acre. Brush stands have been opened up patches reducing cover up to half of pre-burn conditions in monitored locations. Forb production has been maintained and even increased from prior burn conditions. Perennial grasses have doubled in plants per square meter.
Regarding perennial grass recovery, observations indicate an increase in numbers but observations from year 3 shows that many of the plants were seedlings and not yet developing seed heads or were grazed down to 1.5 inches or less. It should be noted that prior to year 3, no livestock grazing occurred in the treated pastures allowing for good recovery and seed head production due to a 2 season rest post treatment. After 2 seasons of rest, livestock was allowed to resume on the allotment. Year 3 observations find very few plants with seed heads persisting occurred unless they were up in rocks or areas that livestock or wildlife were unable to get to. Substantial grazing occurred in those mosaic areas that were treated and were particularly targeted by livestock. The treatment appears to be beneficial to the project area but the continued success of the treatment may depend on a review of livestock management in the allotment.

During the implementation of the RX burn all of the plots received a portion of the treatment. However the entire unit was not treated as the prescription called for a mosaic pattern. All 4 Data Plots were treated with prescribed fire but they are not representative of the whole unit due to the mosaic pattern of the treatment. This was easily achieved since much of the Juniper landscape was not conducive to fire treatment without some prior pretreatment. No juniper pretreatments were attempted when this project was carried out due to the WSA status that much of the project area encompassed. In 2010 the WSA status was dropped and some of the project area was declared wilderness and the northern potion of the project area was simply released from WSA status.

Broadcast Burning
Broadcast burning is the controlled application of fire to wildland fuels within a
predetermined area during specific environmental conditions in order to attain resource
management and fuels reduction objectives. Broadcast burning would be another form of
prescribed fire applied under the proposed action.
Portions of shrub land communities that are in middle to late juniper woodland
transitional stages would require mechanical pretreatment to create ladder fuels that allow
fire to spread. Individual trees would be periodically felled against standing trees and
allowed to cure; creating a ladder allowing ground fire to move into canopies of standing
uncut trees. Sites not supporting large trees typical of communities in earlier stages of
juniper woodland development would not require mechanical treatment prior to
application of prescribed fire. Other pretreatment activities that may occur within or near
broadcast burn units include wet lining, 13 blacklining, jackpot burning, and handline
construction around interior leave islands and fire -sensitive assets such as range
improvements or cultural resources or to decrease heat from the broadcast burn in some
communities. Holding operations near property boundaries may be accomplished with
pretreatment using small amounts of jackpot burning, juniper cutting, and/or piling and
burning.
Scheduling of burning during the 7 to 15-year implementation period is dependent upon
resource objectives, weather, fuel conditions, project funding, and arrangements with
grazing permittees, and other private property owners. These factors, especially weather,
make it difficult to accurately project the number of acres burned in a given year. As
described in PDE #8, broadcast burning operations require one growing season of rest
from livestock grazing prior to treatment and at least two growing seasons of rest
following treatment. The duration of the rest period would be determined by the Field
Manager based on rangeland monitoring by a BLM ID Team of plant community
response.

Objectives: The broadcast burn will be implemented under conditions designed to result in 70-90% of available jackpot fuels ignited.
Planned_Implementation:
2016-Berry Gulch Unit (approx. 1,400 acres): This prescribed fire will use one helicopter.
1. Timberland Helicopter Services will provide the helitorch, mix truck, aircraft, pilot, mechanic and fuel.
• Day One: The helicopter will arrive in Boise the day before the ignition and marry up with the helicopter manager, get a pre-use inspection, load frequencies and obtain a briefing for the next day’s work.
• Day Two: The helicopter will fly to Pole Creek, land, get a briefing from the helibase and burn boss. Required checklists including “Go/No-go” will be completed and checks on the equipment will be made. The helitorch will light the unit. The aircraft will return to Boise at the end of the day.
• Day Three: The helicopter will continue to light the unit as needed. At the end of the day the aircraft can either go to Boise for RON or leave for their home base in Ashland, OR.
Actual_Implementation:
Jackpot burn

3/2/2016
Began ignitions at 1049 in the middle of the unit. Fine Dead Fuel Moisture was at 8, Burning went well worked to the south and west. 250 acres completed.
Stopped burning at 1700
3//3/2016
Began ignitions at 1030, worked to the east and south in the major drainage, 150 Acres completed. Left the unit at 1640.'

3/2/2013 – Arrived on the unit at 1030 to begin jackpot burning the Pole Creek Unit. Soils were very moist with pockets of snow here and there. We lit a test fire on some large juniper in the middle of the unit. Test fire showed that juniper would ignite very easily with consumption of the 1hr and 10hr fuels but limited consumption of the 100hr and 1000hr fuels. We began lighting from the north to south across the unit while working our way back to the west. Ignitions of the jackpots of fuels was not difficult but covering the ground and did take considerably more time than I had anticipated. We burned until 1630-1700 that day and returned back to Boise with about 250 acres completed for the day. We arrived in Boise at 2100.
3/3/2016- We arrived back at the unit at 1000 the next day and picked up burning from where had started the previous day. This time we worked two big draws towards the east, again working north to south across the unit. Several times we had to stop burning and back track to light in a manner that didn’t smoke everyone out. Progress was slow due to the amount of slash that we had to walk through and around. Also waiting for other burners to stay in lightning pattern slowed progress down. The further we got away from vehicles took more time to refuel leading to more lost time. We ended the day with a total of 150 acres completed for the day and returned back to Boise at 2100.
3/7/2016- Weather had moved in to southwest Idaho on 3/4/2016 bringing wide spread rain and snow to the area. I had two people return back to Pole Creek to check the unit but they were only able to get within 15 miles of the unit and had to turn around due to impassable roads. As expected they did not see any obvious signs of fire spread/smoke coming from the unit.
3/14/2016- The weather did turn better for the week but the day that I sent down employees again to check the unit they were unable to access the unit due to impassable roads. No signs of smoke coming from the unit.

corner of DIV Zulu at approximately 1400. All aerial ignitions were completed by 1900 with

Objectives: The jackpot burn will be implemented under conditions designed to result in 70-90% of available jackpot fuels ignited.
Planned_Implementation:
Juniper trees within all units have been pretreated with a combination slashing and girdling. This has created “jackpots” of fuels across the landscape. The juniper trees have been allowed to sit on the ground for anywhere from 1-3 years to cure out prior to ignition and provide for better consumption when ignited. Once cured, the jackpots of trees will be ignited during the late fall to early spring when the risk of spread is low. This treatment allows for only the jackpot fuels to be burned and not the surrounding vegetation. Since burn patches would normally be confined to the individual tree debris zone, most patches would be small (less than two acres), although some larger patches may also occur.

Timberland Helicopter Services will provide the helitorch, mix truck, aircraft, pilot, mechanic and fuel.
Pole Creek: (approximately 2,400 ac).
• Day One (4/9/2018): The helicopter will arrive in Jordan Valley, OR the day before the ignition and marry up with the helicopter manager, get a pre-use inspection, load frequencies and obtain a briefing for the next day’s work.
• Day Two (4/10/2018): The helicopter will fly to Pole Creek, land get a briefing from the helibase and burn boss. Required checklists including “Helitorch Operations Go/No-Go Checklist” will be completed and checks on the equipment will be made. The helitorch will light the unit. The aircraft will return to Jordan Valley at the end of the day.
• Day Three (4/11/2018): The helicopter will continue to light the unit as needed and aim to complete all firing. The aircraft will return to Jordan Valley at the end of the day.
• Day Four (4/12/2018): If all firing was not completed on the prior day and hours are available on the contract then the helicopter will continue to light the unit as needed to complete the unit. It is anticipate that this would be a minimal amount of FT. If all acres are completed then the aircraft will released to Home Unit at the end of the day.
Actual_Implementation:
4/9/2018
At approximately 1030 on April 9, 2018, BLM resources arrived at the Pole Creek Jackpot RX Helibase
and received a briefing. At 1100 aviation personnel conducted pre-use inspections on Helicopter 73U, a
GO/NO GO checklist for helitorch operations was completed, and ground resources drove UTVs out to
the Horse Flat Unit. At 1225 a prescribed fire GO/NO GO checklist was performed and test fire
completed on the northeast corner of the unit. Winds were out of the South at 1-3mph with gusts to
5mph. At 1230 a recon flight was conducted with the pilot and RXB2(t) to familiarize with the burn unit.
Aerial ignitions with the helitorch began at 1300. At 1400 it was determined that only jackpot piles that
had come into direct contact with the burn gel were igniting and the decision was made for the
helicopter to concentrate on the highest density areas of jackpot fuels. Helicopter 73U averaged 3
helitorches per hour before having to refuel. At 1640 the helicopter had a torch malfunction (could not
get wick to light), had to return to helibase and exchange torches for the spare torch, and was on the
ground for approximately 30 minutes. Hand ignitions occurred simultaneously throughout the day in
areas that didn’t affect aerial burning operations. At 1840 ignitions were completed totaling 250 acres
burned for the day. BLM resources returned to Boise and helicopter 73U returned to Jordan Valley, OR.
4/10/2018
All BLM resources briefed at Pole Creek Jackpot RX Helibase at approximately 0915. Ground resources
then drove UTVs out to the Horse Flat Unit. Helicopter 73U arrived at helibase at 1030 and the pilot
voiced concerns over high winds encountered from the ferry flight from Jordan Valley, OR to helibase.
At 1045 a prescribed fire GO/NO GO checklist was completed followed by a test fire near the middle of
the burn unit. Winds on the unit were out of the South at 5-7mph with gusts to 9. Hand ignitions began
promptly after the test fire was completed. Aerial ignitions began at approximately 1215. Aerial
ignitions ended at approximately 1540 due to unfavorable winds between helibase and the burn unit
and helicopter 73U was released from the burn. At 1630 hand ignitions were completed totaling 350
acres burned for the day and BLM resources returned back to Boise.

4/22/18
All resources (13 personnel) were briefed at Pole Creek Jackpot RX Helibase at 0925. Resources then
drove UTVs out to the Horse Flat Unit. At 1115 a GO/NO GO checklist and test fire were completed and
burning conditions were determined to be in prescription. Winds were observed to be 3-5mph w/ gusts
to 7mph out of the northwest. A squad of 5 personnel conducted burning operations near Little Willow
Spring, while remaining personnel started burning at the southeast corner of the unit (within the full-cut
area). At 1322 BDC was contacted and informed that burning operations were on schedule and going
well. At approximately 1400 the squad of five personnel tied back in with the main group to assist with
hand ignitions. At 1635 ignitions were completed totaling 500 acres burned for the day. At 1750 all
UTVs were loaded onto trailers and personnel returned to Boise.

Objectives: Fuels reduction
Planned_Implementation: Prescribed burning could occur in all units.  During winter, spring, or fall piles in accessible areas would be burned using drip torches; some units could be ignited from the air using plastic sphere dispensers or \u201cheli-torches.\u201d  All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and/or horses may be used to transport fire personnel and equipment.  The Proposed Action was designed to minimize surface disturbance by delineating the individual treatment units along natural barriers.  Natural fuel breaks, roads, foam-lines, and hand lines would be used as fire lines when conducting prescribed burns.  Hand lines, if required by the burn plan, would result in surface disturbance.  All constructed lines would be rehabilitated (i.e., water barred and seeded) after the burn.  When feasible, spring burning would use snow fields as natural fire breaks; this would reduce the need for fire line construction.  Where treated areas (particularly aspen stands) are easily accessible to livestock, temporary protective fencing would be erected (e.g., buck and pole fence or trees dropped and jack-strawed around sensitive areas).
